Who lives where in Mexico — a guide to the data

Diversity in a Globalized World

Published

September 9, 2026

What this data is about

The other sessions of this course looked at things crossing borders: goods, people, money, technology. This one stays inside one country and asks a smaller question with a harder answer.

Who lives next to whom?

Mexico is a diverse country. About 7.4 million people speak an indigenous language and 2.6 million identify as Afro-Mexican. But a national average tells you almost nothing about anyone’s actual street. Some municipios are more than half indigenous-speaking. Over a thousand are under 1%. Diversity exists at the level of the country far more than at the level of the neighbourhood.

The same is true of money. Monterrey looks prosperous as a metropolitan area. Inside it, one municipio has a poverty rate of 5% and another has 28%.

This folder covers all 2,469 Mexican municipios, plus 31 metropolitan areas.

The two files

File Use it for What one row is
municipios.rds Maps One municipio
metros.rds Comparing cities One metropolitan area 
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)

municipios <- readRDS("preprocessed_data/municipios.rds")
metros     <- readRDS("preprocessed_data/metros.rds")

municipios.rds — for maps

One row per municipio, with its shape attached. Everything is from 2020.

municipios |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(municipio %in% c("San Pedro Garza García", "El Carmen", "Oaxaca de Juárez")) |>
  select(municipio, state, pop, indigenous_pct, poverty_pct)
               municipio      state    pop indigenous_pct poverty_pct
1              El Carmen Nuevo León 104478       4.001799   28.448074
2 San Pedro Garza García Nuevo León 132169       1.908920    5.450951
3       Oaxaca de Juárez     Oaxaca 270955       7.953719   33.972684
Variable What it means
id Five-digit INEGI municipio code
municipio, state Names
metro_area Which metropolitan area it belongs to, if any (NA if none)
pop Population, 2020
indigenous_language People who speak an indigenous language
indigenous_pct The same, as % of the municipio
afromexican, afromexican_pct People who identify as Afro-Mexican
poverty_pct % of residents in poverty (CONEVAL’s multidimensional measure)
extreme_pct % in extreme poverty
geometry The municipio’s shape — you never touch this directly

A map takes one line:

ggplot(municipios) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = indigenous_pct), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "mako", direction = -1, trans = "sqrt",
                       na.value = "grey90", name = "%") +
  labs(title = "Speakers of an indigenous language, 2020") +
  theme_void()

Swap indigenous_pct for afromexican_pct or poverty_pct and you get a different map of the same country.

Zooming into one city

This is the move that makes the session work. Filter to one metro area and the national map becomes a city map.

mty <- municipios |> filter(metro_area == "Monterrey")

ggplot(mty) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = poverty_pct), color = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "rocket", direction = -1, name = "% poor") +
  labs(title = "Poverty across the Monterrey metro area, 2020") +
  theme_void()

Try "Valle de México", "Guadalajara", "Oaxaca" or any name in metros$metro_area.

metros.rds — for comparing cities

One row per metropolitan area, with segregation already calculated.

metros |> select(metro_area, n_municipios, dissim_poverty, poverty_gap) |> head(5)
# A tibble: 5 × 4
  metro_area      n_municipios dissim_poverty poverty_gap
  <chr>                  <int>          <dbl>       <dbl>
1 Valle de México           76          0.195        67.7
2 Guadalajara                8          0.106        15.2
3 Monterrey                 13          0.138        23.0
4 Puebla-Tlaxcala           39          0.220        54.5
5 Toluca                    15          0.129        32.0
Variable What it means
metro_area Name
n_municipios, pop How many municipios, and total population
dissim_indigenous Index of dissimilarity for indigenous-language speakers
dissim_poverty Index of dissimilarity for people in poverty
poverty_lowest / poverty_highest Poverty rate in its best-off and worst-off municipio
poverty_gap The difference between those two

What the index of dissimilarity means

It answers one question: what share of one group would have to move for the two groups to be spread evenly across the city?

0 means every municipio looks like the metro as a whole. 1 means the two groups share no municipio at all. Monterrey scores 0.26 for indigenous speakers and 0.14 for poverty.

The most important limitation

These are municipios, and municipios are big. Monterrey municipio alone holds over a million people. Averaging across a unit that large smooths away most of the sorting that actually happens, which occurs street by street.

So every segregation number in this folder is a floor, not a ceiling. The real figures are higher. If you report one, say which unit you used and note that a smaller unit would give a bigger number. That sentence is the difference between a good report and a misleading one.

Other things worth knowing

Three municipios have no poverty figure, out of 2,469. They come out grey on a map, which is honest — leave them grey rather than setting them to zero.

indigenous_language counts speakers, not identity. Someone can identify as indigenous without speaking an indigenous language, and the census asks both questions separately. This variable is the language one, so it undercounts.

Poverty here is CONEVAL’s multidimensional measure, not an income line. It combines income with access to education, health services, housing and food. That is why municipal rates look high: the population-weighted national figure is 44%.

Both main variables are lopsided. Indigenous share runs from 0 to 98%, and most municipios are near zero. trans = "sqrt" inside the fill scale keeps the map from being one flat colour.

Questions you could ask

  • Which metro area is most unequal internally, and is it the one you expected?
  • Does the map of indigenous Mexico line up with the map of poor Mexico? Where does it not?
  • Pick your home city. Where does it sit among the 31 metros?
  • Are municipios with more Afro-Mexican residents poorer, richer, or neither?
  • Compare dissim_indigenous with dissim_poverty. Do the same cities top both lists? What would it mean if they did not?
  • Find a municipio that breaks the national pattern, and try to work out why.

Where the data comes from

Population, indigenous language and Afro-Mexican counts: INEGI, Censo de Población y Vivienda 2020, via the mxmaps R package.

Poverty: CONEVAL, Medición de la pobreza a nivel municipio 2020.

Municipio boundaries: mxmaps. We joined the three sources on the five-digit INEGI municipio code, computed the percentage variables and the dissimilarity indices, and attached the shapes.
